title: Security Testing
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and behavior of security testing.
Apply at least one lesson concept—fuzz testing untrusted input—in a small Go example or workflow.
Predict a representative result, then test a boundary case and explain any difference.

content.intro: Security Testing belongs to secure, reliable operation of Go applications. Treat outside data as untrusted, enforce authorization on the server, bound time and resource use, avoid leaking secrets into errors/logs, and validate the resulting behavior with tests and operational signals.
content.why_it_matters: Secure defaults, reliable release procedures, and actionable observability help teams prevent and respond to defects without claiming that a single check guarantees safety.

content_blocks.title: Walk through the example
content_blocks.text: First, identify the input or initial state in the example for security testing. Next, trace the operation or contract that matters, and predict the result before running it. If the example depends on a version-specific feature, a driver, or an external service, follow the stated prerequisites rather than assuming it works in a browser preview.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Adapt the example to one subtopic—Fuzz testing untrusted input—and add a second case that could fail or behave differently. Write down the expected result before testing.

content.task: Create a small example connected to “Security Testing”. Use Fuzz testing untrusted input as the starting point, predict the output, then add one invalid, empty, or boundary case and document its result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates fuzz testing untrusted input or a closely related concept.
Inputs, relevant state changes, and expected output are clear.
At least one boundary case is deliberately tested or documented.
Errors are handled honestly and no success state is reported when the operation fails.
hints: Start from the simplest example related to fuzz testing untrusted input.
Predict the result manually and annotate the value that changes at each step.
Run `gofmt` and the appropriate local `go run`, `go test`, `go vet`, or inspection command when prerequisites are available.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming the happy-path output proves all inputs are safe.
common_mistakes.why: Empty, malformed, boundary, or concurrent cases may follow different paths.
common_mistakes.fix: Add focused tests for a normal input and at least one relevant edge case.

common_mistakes.problem: Ignoring returned errors or external-system status.
common_mistakes.why: Go APIs commonly report expected failures as explicit error values.
common_mistakes.fix: Check errors close to the operation, add useful context when propagating, and clean up resources.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an API or syntax without checking the selected Go version.
common_mistakes.why: Language and standard-library capabilities can change between releases.
common_mistakes.fix: Record `go version`, inspect the `go` directive, and read official release notes for version-specific topics.

summary: Security Testing provides a reusable rule or workflow for Go programs.
The subtopics to revisit are: Fuzz testing untrusted input; Testing authorization boundaries; Malformed input testing; Race-condition testing; Security regression tests.
Prefer a small reproducible example, explicit errors, appropriate tests, and version-matched official documentation.
